slides.title: Signal Processing
slides.notes: Open by naming the central tension of the chapter: graphics code stores arrays, but the visual quantities we care about are functions of time, position, direction, or surface coordinates. The lecture should make sampling feel like an engineering contract rather than a file format. Every later image operation will ask which frequencies, averages, and invariants survived the conversion to samples.

slides.title: From Functions to Arrays
slides.notes: Use this slide to separate mathematical type from storage type. An image array is familiar, but it is only one example of a sampled function. Emphasize that the same ideas apply to digitizer motion, volume data, texture maps, shadow maps, and displays. The warning matters because students often judge an algorithm by a plotted line even though the algorithm only received discrete measurements.

slides.title: Aliasing
slides.notes: Spend time on the word story. The samples are identical, so the distinction between the two continuous curves is no longer present in the data. This is stronger than saying the reconstruction looks bad. It says the renderer has destroyed information before reconstruction begins. The practical fix is to avoid admitting frequencies that the sampling lattice cannot represent.

slides.title: Reconstruction Choices
slides.notes: After aliasing, this slide makes a second distinction: even when the samples are accepted as the data, a renderer still has to define values between them. Zero-order hold, linear reconstruction, cubic filters, and windowed sinc filters all answer the same question differently. Remind students that smoother is not automatically more correct if the missing frequency content was never sampled.

slides.title: Convolution Local Average
slides.notes: Introduce convolution first as something concrete: place the filter over nearby samples, multiply, and add. The flipped index can be acknowledged without making it the whole lecture. The essential instructor point is the invariant. A blur kernel whose weights sum to one should not darken a constant image, and that simple check catches many implementation mistakes.

slides.title: Convolution Algebra
slides.notes: Switch viewpoints deliberately. The local average view explains how to compute one output; the shifted-copy view explains the whole output and prepares students for reconstruction filters. This is a good moment to connect algebra to debugging. If a convolution implementation is not commutative, associative in the tested cases, or identity-preserving with an impulse, there is likely an indexing or boundary mistake.

slides.title: Discrete Continuous Convolution
slides.notes: Use this as the conceptual bridge from arrays to curves and images. Students should see that reconstruction is not magic interpolation between neighboring points. It is a sum of continuous basis functions. The filter support controls how many samples participate at each position, while the filter smoothness controls the regularity of the reconstructed function.

slides.title: Filter Gallery
slides.notes: Do not present the gallery as a ranking. Each filter answers a different design pressure. Box and tent are simple and cheap. Gaussian filtering is an excellent way to reduce high frequencies before sampling. Cubic and windowed-sinc families can look sharper, but their negative lobes make ringing a predictable risk. The goal is to read the artifact from the filter shape.

slides.title: Filter Properties
slides.notes: Tie this slide directly to the notebook ledger. A filter diagram alone is not enough; students should ask how it behaves on constants, at integer locations, at boundaries, and near discontinuities. The ripple-free condition is especially useful because it turns an abstract reconstruction property into a concrete sum over shifted filters.

slides.title: 2D Convolution
slides.notes: Now move from signals to images without changing the mental model. A 2D convolution still multiplies a neighborhood by weights and sums. The separability point is worth emphasizing because it shows why mathematical structure matters in production code. A Gaussian-like blur can be dramatically cheaper when implemented as horizontal and vertical passes.

slides.title: Image Processing
slides.notes: This slide should make image processing feel less like a list of software features and more like reusable signal algebra. Blurring, sharpening, and shadows differ in purpose, but each can be described by filtering, adding, shifting, or compositing filtered signals. Point out that the notebook uses a synthetic image so visual observations can be paired with measurable variance and high-pass energy checks.

slides.title: Image Aliasing
slides.notes: Make the prefiltering order explicit. Antialiasing is not a cosmetic blur added after the wrong samples have already been chosen. The filter must be part of the sampling process so the stored value represents an average over a footprint. This slide also prepares students for texture filtering, where the footprint may be much larger or more elongated than one pixel.

slides.title: Resampling
slides.notes: Frame resizing as a sampling problem, not as a pixel-selection problem. The input samples define a reconstructed function, and the output pixels sample that function. When the target has fewer samples, the filter must become wider to remove frequencies that would alias. This explains why nearest neighbor can look crisp while being spectrally wrong.

slides.title: Fourier View
slides.notes: Introduce the Fourier view as a diagnostic tool, not as a new topic disconnected from filtering. In space, convolution is a weighted average and can be visually local. In frequency, the same operation is multiplication by the filter response. That makes it much easier to explain why a Gaussian damps high frequencies smoothly and why poor reconstruction filters leak alias spectra.

slides.title: Spectrum Aliasing
slides.notes: This is the key sampling-theory slide. Ask students to look for overlap, not for individual waves. Sampling creates periodic copies of the spectrum, and the sample rate controls the spacing between those copies. Once overlap occurs, the mixture is built into the stored samples. Low-pass filtering before sampling narrows the spectrum so the copies interfere less.

slides.title: Frequency Response
slides.notes: Compare the response curves qualitatively. The box filter has broad side lobes, so it leaves visible reconstruction artifacts. The tent response rolls off more strongly because it is a box convolved with itself. Gaussian response falls smoothly, which is why it is attractive for prefiltering. Then make the practical point: ideal frequency behavior is not the same as ideal image appearance or runtime.

slides.title: Notebook Checks
slides.notes: Use the lab slide to model how students should write signal-processing explanations. A picture can be persuasive but misleading; an invariant can be correct but hard to interpret. The best report names both. For example, a downsampled image may look sharp because it kept high frequencies, while the spectrum and constant-preservation checks show whether the method respected the new sampling grid.

slides.title: Signal Processing Recap
slides.notes: Close by turning the chapter into a debugging habit. Whenever a renderer resizes, filters, stores, or reconstructs a signal, ask what the sample lattice can represent and what the filter preserves. The chapter is not just about Fourier plots; it is about making image and texture operations predictable by tracking averages, frequencies, and invariants.
